title: Separation of Concerns
learningObjectives: Explain why distinct responsibilities should be separated.
Identify mixed responsibilities in a small program.
Group code by purpose without overcomplicating it.
Describe how separation improves change and testing.
Apply a simple separation to a practical example.

understand.concept: Separation of concerns means organizing a program so different responsibilities are handled in distinct places. A concern might be input collection, validation, calculation, storage, or display. Keeping these responsibilities apart reduces the chance that changing one area breaks another and makes each part easier to test. Separation is a spectrum: a small script may need only a few clear functions, while a larger application may use modules or layers. The goal is clarity and manageable change, not maximum file count.
understand.whyItMatters: Focused responsibilities and controlled boundaries make software easier to change, test, and explain.
understand.analogy: A well-organized workshop keeps tools and tasks arranged so each job can be completed without disturbing unrelated work.
understand.analogyLimit: Real software components exchange data and have technical constraints that a physical workshop analogy cannot fully capture.

explain.narrative: When a function both parses input, calculates a result, writes to storage, and prints a message, it is difficult to reuse or test. Divide the workflow into meaningful responsibilities and pass data between them explicitly. Keep boundaries lightweight for small tasks and introduce stronger boundaries as complexity grows.

examples.title: Separate calculation from display
examples.explanation: The calculation can be reused without printing.

examples.title: Format output in its own function
Pass data across a boundary
examples.explanation: The function accepts data and returns a result without depending on UI.

examples.title: Keep orchestration readable
examples.explanation: The run function coordinates work while calculation remains separate.

commonMistakes: Making boundaries too small or too large without a reason.
Allowing components to rely on hidden state.
Mixing unrelated responsibilities in one function.
Exposing internal data that callers can modify unexpectedly.
Treating a design guideline as a rigid rule instead of a contextual trade-off.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: Identify the input, validation, calculation, and output steps in a small program. Create one focused function for calculation. Move validation into a small function if it improves clarity. Keep the main flow readable and pass values explicitly. Trace the output and note which responsibility could change independently.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Create a simple receipt calculator. Separate input assumptions, validation, calculation, and display formatting. Use at least three focused functions. Show that the calculation function can be called with different inputs. Explain one change that would now be easier to make.

Use at least three focused functions.
Show that the calculation function can be called with different inputs.
Explain one change that would now be easier to make.

hints: Separate responsibilities that change for different reasons.
Functions should have clear inputs and outputs.
Avoid splitting tiny code into meaningless fragments.
Pass data rather than relying on hidden global state.
Choose boundaries based on clarity and expected change.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of separation of concerns?
options: Keep different responsibilities manageable
Make every function one line
Remove all communication between parts
Increase file count
questions.explanation: Distinct responsibilities can change and be tested more independently.

questions.prompt: Which function is easiest to reuse?
options: A calculation function that returns a value
A function that reads globals and prints
A function that does every task
A function with unrelated side effects
questions.answer: A calculation function that returns a value
questions.explanation: A focused function is easier to reuse in different contexts.

options: No; boundaries should match complexity and clarity
Yes, every line needs a module
No functions should be used
Only large programs need readable code
questions.answer: No; boundaries should match complexity and clarity
questions.explanation: Overengineering can make a simple task harder to follow.

questions.prompt: What is a concern in a program?
options: A distinct responsibility such as validation or display
A random variable
Only an error
A programming language
questions.answer: A distinct responsibility such as validation or display
questions.explanation: Concerns represent responsibilities or areas of behavior.

options: Parts can often be tested independently
It removes the need for tests
It guarantees no bugs
It hides inputs
questions.answer: Parts can often be tested independently
questions.explanation: Focused units have clearer test setup and expectations.
